verses.text: And Joseph fell upon his father’s face, and wept upon him, and kissed him.
And Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father: and the physicians embalmed Israel.
And forty days were fulfilled for him; for so are fulfilled the days of those which are embalmed: and the Egyptians mourned for him threescore and ten days.
And when the days of his mourning were past, Joseph spake unto the house of Pharaoh, saying, If now I have found grace in your eyes, speak, I pray you, in the ears of Pharaoh, saying,

My father made me swear, saying, Lo, I die: in my grave which I have digged for me in the land of Canaan, there shalt thou bury me. Now therefore let me go up, I pray thee, and bury my father, and I will come again.
And Pharaoh said, Go up, and bury thy father, according as he made thee swear.
And Joseph went up to bury his father: and with him went up all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his house, and all the elders of the land of Egypt,
And all the house of Joseph, and his brethren, and his father’s house: only their little ones, and their flocks, and their herds, they left in the land of Goshen.
And there went up with him both chariots and horsemen: and it was a very great company.
And they came to the threshingfloor of Atad, which is beyond Jordan, and there they mourned with a great and very sore lamentation: and he made a mourning for his father seven days.

And when the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning in the floor of Atad, they said, This is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians: wherefore the name of it was called Abel-mizraim, which is beyond Jordan.
And his sons did unto him according as he commanded them:

For his sons carried him into the land of Canaan, and buried him in the cave of the field of Machpelah, which Abraham bought with the field for a possession of a buryingplace of Ephron the Hittite, before Mamre.
And Joseph returned into Egypt, he, and his brethren, and all that went up with him to bury his father, after he had buried his father.
And when Joseph’s brethren saw that their father was dead, they said, Joseph will peradventure hate us, and will certainly requite us all the evil which we did unto him.
And they sent a messenger unto Joseph, saying, Thy father did command before he died, saying,

So shall ye say unto Joseph, Forgive, I pray thee now, the trespass of thy brethren, and their sin; for they did unto thee evil: and now, we pray thee, forgive the trespass of the servants of the God of thy father. And Joseph wept when they spake unto him.
And his brethren also went and fell down before his face; and they said, Behold, we be thy servants.
And Joseph said unto them, Fear not: for am I in the place of God?
But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
Now therefore fear ye not: I will nourish you, and your little ones. And he comforted them, and spake kindly unto them.
And Joseph dwelt in Egypt, he, and his father’s house: and Joseph lived an hundred and ten years.
And Joseph saw Ephraim’s children of the third generation: the children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were brought up upon Joseph’s knees.
And Joseph said unto his brethren, I die: and God will surely visit you, and bring you out of this land unto the land which he sware to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.
And Joseph took an oath of the children of Israel, saying, God will surely visit you, and ye shall carry up my bones from hence.
So Joseph died, being an hundred and ten years old: and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt.

chapters.summary: Genesis closes at the graveside. Joseph falls on his dead father's face weeping, then has the physicians embalm him over forty days, and Egypt mourns Jacob seventy days. Gaining Pharaoh's leave, Joseph leads a great funeral procession — "all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his house," chariots and horsemen — up to Canaan. At the threshingfloor of Atad they mourn so grievously the Canaanites name the place Abel-mizraim. His sons bury Jacob in the cave of Machpelah, the ancestral burying place, and return to Egypt. With their father gone, the brothers fear reprisal: "Joseph will peradventure hate us, and will certainly requite us all the evil which we did." They send word begging forgiveness, and Joseph weeps. When they fall before him offering to be his servants, he gives the book's climactic word of grace: "Fear not: for am I in the place of God? But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive." He comforts them and pledges to nourish them. Joseph lives to 110, sees his great-grandchildren, and dying, looks beyond Egypt: "God will surely visit you, and bring you out of this land" to the promised land. He binds Israel by oath to carry up his bones. "So Joseph died... and he was put in a coffin in Egypt."
takeaways: Joseph's final word to his brothers crowns the book's theology: "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good."
True forgiveness refuses the seat of judgment — "am I in the place of God?" — leaving vengeance to the Lord.
Genesis ends on hope deferred: Joseph dies in a coffin in Egypt, trusting God will "surely visit" and bring Israel home.
The oath about Joseph's bones binds the book forward to the Exodus, keeping the promise of the land alive.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 45:5-8 — God sent me to preserve life
crossRefs.why: Joseph's climactic "God meant it unto good" restates and confirms what he first told his brothers at the reunion: God sent him ahead to preserve life. The repetition after Jacob's death seals the providence theme as the settled meaning of his suffering.

crossRefs.label: Romans 12:19-21 — leave vengeance to God, overcome evil with good
crossRefs.why: Paul urges believers not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's judgment and overcome evil with good. Joseph's refusal to "requite" his brothers, asking "am I in the place of God?", is a living model of that ethic.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 13:19 — Moses carries Joseph's bones
crossRefs.why: Joseph made Israel swear to carry his bones out of Egypt, and Exodus records Moses fulfilling that oath at the Exodus. The dying charge here reaches directly into the deliverance to come, binding Genesis to Israel's redemption.

crossRefs.label: Hebrews 11:22 — Joseph's faith about the departure from Egypt
crossRefs.why: Hebrews commends that "by faith Joseph, when he died, made mention of the departing of the children of Israel; and gave commandment concerning his bones." It reads his final words as an act of faith in God's promise of the land.

interpretationNotes.claim: Joseph's declaration that God turned intended evil into good is read as a classic statement of divine providence, and his freely offered forgiveness prefigures the reconciling mercy of Christ toward those who wronged him.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readers likewise treat this verse as a keystone text on providence and God's sovereignty over human evil, often pairing it with Romans 8:28. Both traditions affirm that God's good purpose does not excuse the brothers' sin, and both see Joseph's mercy as an exemplar of forgiveness; the Christ-typology is widely shared though emphasized in varying degrees.
